newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-TRIBUTES FLOW AS GENTLEMAN EDBERG BOWS OUT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-TRIBUTES FLOW AS GENTLEMAN EDBERG BOWS OUT.

text.p: Tributes flowed in on Wednesday as Stefan Edberg, the gentleman of world tennis, bowed out of the international circuit after 14 years at the top.
"The game is going to miss one of the all-time best players and a great ambassador," ATP Tour chief executive officer Mark Miles said.
"One of the true greats of Swedish sport," said Swedish tabloid Aftonbladet.

In a rare display of emotion, the usually reserved Swede unsuccessfully fought back the tears as a rapturous home crowd rose to its feet to bid him farewell from the Stockholm's centre court for the final time on Tuesday.
"It was a little heartbreaking," Edberg later told a press conference at the Sweden's Royal Tennis Club.
"At the same time I was also a little relieved that this part of playing tournaments is over."

The 30-year-old, world number one in 1990 and 1991, announced his impending retirement from competition tennis in late 1995 to spend more time with his wife and three-year-old daughter Emilie and pursue other interests.
Edberg lists those interests as golf and business, with a range of investments from shares to real estate.
He acknowledged that his final match was a little disappointing, losing to fellow Swede Nicklas Kulti in 80 minutes in the first round of the Stockholm Open 7-6 6-3.
"I had hopes coming into this tournament and felt quite good about myself," said Edberg. "It was a shame."
Although the Stockholm Open was Edberg's last singles tournament, he is still hoping to represent his country in the Davis Cup final against France in Malmo in late November.
"It is not quite over," he said.
Discovered by Bjorn Borg's coach Percy Rosberg, Edberg turned pro in 1983 and won his first title in Milan in 1984.
Edberg never looked back, winning 806 of 1,075 games with 41 tournament victories and six Grand Slam titles that have earned him over $20 million in prize money.
He has now set up his own foundation in Sweden to help the budding Edbergs of the future.
Always one of the true gentlemen of the game, Edberg was popular amoung tennis buffs and competitors alike.
"I have respect for Stefan as he can return every ball I play and still is able to play offensively," Andre Agassi once said of Edberg.
"I really like him. Even as a boy I thought he was special and I hoped we would play doubles together for many years," said Czech player and occasional doubles partner Petr Korda.
Edberg has kept himself steadfastly out of the gossip columns, and on court never succumbed to the temper and tantrums displayed by some of his rivals.
Edberg, who has lived in London since 1984, appeared to have no regrets about his retirement even though his final departure was difficult.
"A few months off will be next for me," Edberg said. "I've said to myself I will have time over Christmas and New Year and will think about what I want to do."
